Dynamic programming. An algorithmic technique that solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, storing the results to avoid redundant recomputation, and building solutions upward from base cases. It transforms inefficient recursive approaches—often exponential in complexity—into polynomial-time algorithms by trading space for speed. Dynamic programming excels at optimization problems where decisions must be made sequentially and subproblems recur throughout the solution.

Two principles make dynamic programming work. Optimal substructure means the optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems. Overlapping subproblems means the same subproblems are computed many times in a naive recursive approach. Dynamic programming computes each once and caches the result. Two implementation styles exist: memoization, which is top-down recursion with caching, and tabulation, which is bottom-up iterative table-filling.

Classic examples illustrate dynamic programming's power. The Fibonacci sequence is naive recursion O of two to the n, but dynamic programming memoization or tabulation reduces it to O of n. The longest increasing subsequence problem finds the longest ordered subsequence in an array; dynamic programming solves it in O of n squared or O of n log n with binary search. The zero-one knapsack problem selects items with maximum value subject to a weight constraint; dynamic programming solves it in O of n times W, where W is the weight limit. Edit distance, or Levenshtein distance, computes the minimum insertions, deletions, or substitutions to transform one string into another; dynamic programming is O of m times n. The coin change problem finds the minimum number of coins to make a target value; dynamic programming is O of n times amount.

Memoization recursively solves subproblems and stores results in a hash table. The algorithm recurses only if the result is not cached. Tabulation builds a table bottom-up, filling cells in dependency order. There is no recursion stack, just explicit control flow. For problems like the longest increasing subsequence or coin change, the full table is unnecessary. Rolling arrays or single-dimension arrays can reduce space from O of n squared to O of n or even O of one.

Dynamic programming emerged from control theory and operations research but has become central to computer science practice. It exemplifies a fundamental principle: invest space upfront to save time later. Without dynamic programming, many practical problems—sequence alignment in computational biology, speech recognition, resource scheduling—would be computationally infeasible.
